source.title: Scaling Laws for Code: A More Data-Hungry Regime
source.authors: Xian-Zhen Luo; Wen-Zheng Zheng; Qing-Fu Zhu; Rongyin Zhang; Houyi Li; Siming Huang; Yuantao Fan; Wan-Xiang Che

record.file_problem: The full paper text is supplied. Some table and figure material is flattened, but the main results and the validation table are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out pretraining loss across model and data scales and fits scaling laws, using the same general loss-versus-scale measurement as the original work in a new code-pretraining setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scale sweeps, fitted-law comparisons, three fixed-compute validation runs, and code/NL mixture results. The NL scaling surfaces used for comparison are not new experiments by this study and are not recorded as results. Values for the 117-run sweeps and mixture surfaces are not individually stated in the text, so those results are recorded only at the aggregate level or as figure-only findings.
record.test_reason: The study trains 117 decoder-only models on a curated code corpus (N 0.2–3.18B non-embedding, D 2–128B). It measures held-out code validation loss and fits Chinchilla- and Farseer-form laws. It then checks predictions at a larger compute budget (5.36e21 FLOPs) and derives compute-optimal D/N. The method matches the originals' loss-vs-scale approach, applied to a new data domain (code), so T3 fits better than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that code loss is highly predictable and best modelled by the Farseer law, which beats Chinchilla in both fit and validation error. They find that code scales robustly with N but is data-hungry: its compute-optimal D/N is well above NL's and the gap widens with compute. NL mixing helps only in low-resource settings and hurts at larger scale. They also stress that the fitted parameters are setup-specific, not universal.
record.recipe_differences: Applies Chinchilla and Farseer loss-law fitting to code pretraining with a consistent decoder-only architecture, 117 budget-conscious configurations, and a held-out code validation set. The study adds code/NL mixture sweeps; it is not a full replication of the larger Farseer experiment design.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted optimal D/N trend depends on the chosen law: the paper describes the Chinchilla fit as giving linear growth and Farseer as giving super-linear growth. Mixture outcomes vary with model size, code-token D/N ratio, and compute regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding NL data lowers code validation loss only for small models or code-scarce regimes (e.g. N=31.6M at D/N<40; N<0.1B at D/N=18.3). The benefit vanishes or reverses as N or the code-token count grows. Several slices are extrapolated below the fitted N range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of cross-domain data mixing for in-domain loss depends on scale and reverses at higher compute.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study uses 117 fitting configurations rather than the 400+ configurations in the cited Farseer study. Its fixed-compute validation covers three D/N ratios at one compute budget and does not reach the largest industrial scales. Mixture experiments test only two ratios. Mixture-surface values are primarily shown in figures, and no statistical uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Individual outcomes for the 117 pure-code runs and the 234 mixture runs are not separately stated in the supplied text; Figures 3 and 6–7 show aggregate trends or fitted surfaces, so those individual points are not transcribed as separate rows. Figure 7's N=173M slice is mentioned qualitatively but not retained as a separate row because the text says mixture advantages almost completely vanish there and gives the more decisive N=0.94B comparison in r11.

untested.parts: Ranges beyond about 1.2 orders of magnitude in N and 1.8 in D; compute as a separate axis; NL-only data.
Extrapolation by orders of magnitude. Validation reaches only about 2× the largest fitted compute and 2× the largest N.
Empirical compute-optimal N and D measured across several budgets. Only one budget, with three ratios, was run.
Not tested. Architecture shape is fixed by the Farseer procedure.
Not tested. Code is text-token language-model pretraining (covered under V1). No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling is studied. Code/NL mixtures are a data-mix comparison.
Not tested. No downstream tasks are evaluated.
Parameter-counting conventions, schedules and fitting procedures beyond the choice of law form are not varied.

missing.what: Fitted Chinchilla parameters for code: E=0.2193, A=534.374, a=0.4853, B=76.0743, b=0.2983 (D exponent smaller than N exponent). Also the full Farseer parameters.
The two laws imply different irreducible losses on the same data: 0.2193 (Chinchilla) vs about 8.0e-7 (Farseer).
Code vs NL scaling shape: gains from N are larger for code than NL, D-scaling is less efficient for code, and the NL surface flattens sooner. Figure-only; the NL surface comes from prior work.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T3 because code is a new data domain. V5 is set to untested because code pretraining is still text-token LM pretraining, and the mixture rows measure mixing benefit, not the scaling form. Validation extrapolation is modest, so the orders-of-magnitude part of V2 is untested. Figure 7 slices at N=31.6M and N<0.1B lie below the 0.2B minimum training size and are extrapolations of the fitted surfaces. Compute is reported as 13,600 H100 GPU-days in the main text but A100 GPU-days in Appendix C. Figure 1's comparison of public code LLMs is observational and cited, not a result row.

versions.untested_parts: Natural-language-only results and behavior outside the tested code models, corpus, and stated N and D ranges.
Extrapolation to industrial-scale runs and to several orders of magnitude beyond the measured configurations.
The study derives an optimal D/N trend, but does not report separate empirical power-law exponents for optimal N and D across compute budgets.
No controlled comparison varies depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
No downstream task performance is evaluated.

The study compares Chinchilla and Farseer fits, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, schedules, datasets, or fitting procedures; it does not test curve bending outside the studied range.

rows.subject: Code model, D/N=20
rows.operation_detail: Compared fitted-law loss predictions with measured validation loss at a fixed compute budget.
rows.measure: Validation loss; fitted predictions and relative errors
rows.note: This is the NL Chinchilla-optimal D/N comparison point; the observed loss is higher than at D/N=150.
rows.check: Remove V1 and V3: a single point at one budget cannot show a power law or growth of the optimum with compute. For V2, the Farseer error is 9.49‰ (about 0.95%), while Chinchilla overpredicts by 34.55‰. The row should be split by law. The extrapolation is modest: N=6.37B is 2× the largest fitted N, and C is about 2.2× the largest fitted run (3.18B×128B×6≈2.4e21). For V7, D/N=20 (the NL-optimal ratio) gives higher loss (0.256833) than D/N=150 (0.253786).

rows.subject: Code Farseer fit (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Derived compute-optimal D/N from the fitted code scaling surface and compared it across compute budgets.
rows.baseline: NL curves; numerical values not stated
rows.value: The text says code's optimal D/N is consistently higher than NL's, the gap widens with scale, and code's optimal D/N grows super-linearly with C; curve values are figure only.
rows.note: The figure compares fitted-law predictions; it is not a sweep of empirical optima at many compute budgets.
rows.check: This is derived from the fitted laws (Figure 5), not from empirical optima across budgets. For V7 the effect is observed: the optimal split differs between code and NL, and between laws (Chinchilla fit linear on log axes, Farseer super-linear). For V3 it is partial: under the better-fitting Farseer form, optimal D/N rises super-linearly with C, so the allocation is not a stable power. The fitted D/N rising with C also matches neither the Kaplan nor the Hoffmann split.

source_check.correct: V7: observed differences between fitted allocation curves across data and law forms. V3: fitted-law qualification of the constant-ratio prescription; stable allocation powers and empirical optima across budgets are not established.
source_check.problem: A single partial state obscures the observed V7 effect and the narrower, fit-derived evidence concerning V3.
